days.lesson:
Diabetes mellitus is a chronic disease in which the body cannot properly regulate blood sugar (glucose). Glucose is the body's main source of energy. It comes from food and enters body cells with the help of a hormone called insulin. When insulin does not work properly or the body cannot produce enough insulin, glucose builds up in the blood. Over time, high blood sugar can damage: • Eyes • Kidneys • Nerves • Heart • Blood vessels Key Message:
  • Diabetes is serious but often preventable.

Topic
Signs and Symptoms of Diabetes
Educational Lesson
Common symptoms include:
• Excessive thirst
• Frequent urination
• Excessive hunger
• Unexplained weight loss
• Fatigue
• Blurred vision
Some people experience no symptoms for years.
Interactive Activity
Symptom Recognition Quiz
Symptom Recognition Quiz: Could You Recognize Diabetes Warning Signs?
Instructions: Select the correct answer for each question.
Question 1
Which of the following is a common symptom of diabetes?
A. Increased energy
B. Excessive thirst
C. Better eyesight
D. Reduced appetite
✅ Correct Answer: B. Excessive thirst
Explanation: High blood glucose levels can cause the body to lose more water, leading to increased thirst.

Question 2
A person with diabetes may experience frequent urination because:
A. The body tries to remove excess glucose through urine
B. The person drinks too little water
C. The kidneys stop working immediately
D. The person exercises too much
✅ Correct Answer: A. The body tries to remove excess glucose through urine
Explanation: When blood glucose levels are high, the kidneys work to remove excess sugar, causing frequent urination.

Question 3
Which combination of symptoms may suggest a possible diabetes warning sign?
A. Excessive thirst, frequent urination, and unexplained weight loss
B. Increased strength and improved vision
C. Better sleep and increased energy
D. Reduced hunger and weight gain
✅ Correct Answer: A. Excessive thirst, frequent urination, and unexplained weight loss
Explanation: These are common signs that may occur when blood glucose levels are not well controlled.

Question 4
True or False:
"Everyone with Type 2 diabetes will notice symptoms immediately."
A. True
B. False
✅ Correct Answer: B. False
Explanation: Some people with Type 2 diabetes may have no symptoms for years, which is why awareness and regular screening are important.

Remember the warning signs:
💧 Excessive thirst
🚽 Frequent urination
🍽️ Excessive hunger
⚖️ Unexplained weight loss
😴 Fatigue
👁️ Blurred vision
Early recognition can support early testing, prevention, and better health outcomes.

Reflection Question
Have you ever experienced any of these symptoms?

days.lesson:
Many people believe that diabetes occurs suddenly or only affects older adults. However, Type 2 diabetes develops gradually over several years as a result of a combination of risk factors. A risk factor is anything that increases the likelihood of developing a disease. Having one or more risk factors does not mean that a person will definitely develop diabetes, but it increases the chances. Risk factors for Type 2 diabetes can be divided into two categories: Non-Modifiable Risk Factors:
  • These are factors that cannot be changed.
  • 1. Family History
  • People whose parents or siblings have diabetes are at higher risk.
  • 2. Age
  • Risk generally increases with age, although young adults are increasingly affected.
  • 3. Ethnicity
  • Certain populations, including many African populations, have higher susceptibility to Type 2 diabetes.
Modifiable Risk Factors:
  • These are factors that individuals can change.
  • 1. Overweight and Obesity
  • Excess body fat, especially around the abdomen, increases insulin resistance.
  • 2. Physical Inactivity
  • Lack of regular exercise reduces the body's ability to use insulin effectively.
  • 3. Unhealthy Diet
  • Frequent consumption of sugary drinks, fast foods, and highly processed foods contributes to weight gain and diabetes risk.
  • 4. Smoking
  • Smoking damages blood vessels and increases insulin resistance.
  • 5. Excessive Alcohol Consumption
  • Heavy alcohol use affects blood glucose regulation and body weight.
  • Why University Students Should Care:
  • Many university students experience:
  • Long hours of sitting during lectures
  • Frequent consumption of sugary drinks
  • Irregular meal patterns
  • High stress levels
  • Inadequate physical activity
  • These habits can gradually increase diabetes risk.
Key Takeaway:
  • Type 2 diabetes often develops silently. Understanding your risk factors allows you to take preventive action early.

days.lesson:
One of the strongest predictors of Type 2 diabetes is family history. Genes influence how the body: • Produces insulin • Uses insulin • Stores body fat • Regulates blood sugar If one or both parents have diabetes, your risk is higher than someone without a family history. However, genetics is not destiny. Think of genes as loading the gun and lifestyle as pulling the trigger. A person with a family history who maintains healthy habits may never develop diabetes, while a person without a family history may develop diabetes due to unhealthy lifestyle choices. Family History Categories: Low Risk: • No parent or sibling has diabetes. Moderate Risk: • One close relative has diabetes. High Risk: • Multiple close relatives have diabetes. Why Knowing Family History Matters:
  • Knowing your family history allows you to:
  • Screen earlier
  • Improve lifestyle habits
  • Monitor weight
  • Seek preventive care
Key Takeaway:
  • You cannot change your genes, but you can change your lifestyle.

days.lesson:
Excess body fat, especially around the waist, increases the risk of developing Type 2 diabetes. Fat tissue is not just a storage site for energy. It releases substances that affect insulin action. When excess fat accumulates: • Cells become resistant to insulin. • Blood glucose rises. • The pancreas works harder. • Diabetes risk increases. Why Waist Size Matters: Abdominal fat is particularly dangerous because it is strongly associated with insulin resistance. **Low Risk (Healthy):** • For men, a waist circumference of 37 inches (94 cm) or less is considered low risk. • For women, a waist circumference of 31.5 inches (80 cm) or less is considered low risk. **Increased Risk:** • For men, a waist circumference of 37.1–39.9 inches (94.1–101.9 cm) indicates increased risk. • For women, a waist circumference of 31.6–34.9 inches (80.1–87.9 cm) indicates increased risk. **High Risk (Abdominal Obesity):** • For men, a waist circumference of 40 inches (102 cm) or more indicates high risk. • For women, a waist circumference of 35 inches (88 cm) or more indicates high risk. Key Takeaway:
  • Maintaining a healthy weight significantly reduces diabetes risk.

Alcohol provides empty calories, meaning it contains energy but provides little or no essential nutrients such as vitamins, minerals, or fibre.   • Increasing calorie intake and contributing to weight gain.
  • Affecting blood sugar control, especially when combined with unhealthy eating habits.

Alcohol can also affect decision-making, making it harder to maintain healthy lifestyle choices such as choosing nutritious foods or staying physically active. Why This Matters: Maintaining a healthy weight and lifestyle reduces your risk of developing Type 2 diabetes. Understanding how alcohol affects your body helps you make informed choices.

Getting enough sleep is important, but sleep quality also matters. Good sleep hygiene involves developing habits that help your body prepare for restful sleep. Tips for improving sleep quality include:
  • Maintain a consistent bedtime: Going to bed and waking up at similar times helps regulate your body clock.
  • Reduce screen time before bed: Phones, laptops, and other devices can make it harder to fall asleep.
  • Limit caffeine intake: Drinks such as coffee, energy drinks, and some soft drinks can interfere with sleep, especially when consumed late in the day.
  • Create a relaxing bedtime routine: Activities such as reading, stretching, or quiet reflection can prepare your body for sleep.
Why This Matters:
  • Better sleep supports healthier eating habits, energy levels, stress management, and diabetes prevention.

days.lesson:
Relaxation techniques help calm the mind and reduce the body’s stress response. Practicing relaxation regularly can improve emotional wellbeing and help you manage daily challenges. Some effective relaxation methods include:
  • Deep Breathing: Slow, controlled breathing can reduce tension and help the body relax.
  • Stretching: Gentle stretching helps release muscle tension caused by stress and prolonged sitting.
  • Mindfulness: Paying attention to the present moment without judgment can improve focus and emotional control.
These techniques can be practiced anywhere, during study breaks, before sleeping, or during stressful situations. Why This Matters:
  • Healthy stress management can prevent unhealthy coping behaviors and support better lifestyle choices.

  • Improve emotional regulation.
  • Reduce stress and anxiety.
  • Improve concentration and self-awareness.
  • Support healthier responses to challenges.

  • Improving mental wellbeing supports healthier decisions related to eating, physical activity, sleep, and overall diabetes prevention.

questions.question: What is stress?
options: A. A disease that only affects older adults
B. The body’s response to challenges or demands

questions.question: How can chronic stress increase the risk of Type 2 diabetes?

B. By lowering blood glucose permanently
C. By increasing blood glucose and encouraging unhealthy behaviors

days.lesson:
Habits are behaviors that you repeat regularly until they become automatic. Healthy habits help you make good choices without having to think about them every day. Building positive habits can reduce your risk of developing Type 2 diabetes and improve your overall health. Healthy habits do not have to be difficult. Small, consistent actions practiced daily often lead to lasting lifestyle changes. Examples of Healthy Habits
  • Drink enough water throughout the day.
  • Walk or exercise for at least 30 minutes most days.
  • Eat vegetables with your meals.
  • Choose healthy snacks instead of sugary foods.
  • Get enough sleep each night.
Why It Matters: Healthy habits improve blood sugar control, support a healthy weight, increase energy, and reduce the risk of chronic diseases.

days.lesson:
Setting clear goals makes healthy behavior easier to achieve. SMART goals help you focus on realistic changes and measure your progress. A SMART goal is:
  • Specific – Clearly state what you want to do.
  • Measurable – Track your progress.
  • Achievable – Make sure it is realistic.
  • Relevant – Choose a goal that supports your health.
  • Time-bound – Set a deadline.
Example "I will walk for 30 minutes after class on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday for the next four weeks." Why It Matters: SMART goals increase confidence, improve commitment, and make it easier to build healthy habits over time.

days.lesson:
Changing your lifestyle is a journey, and occasional setbacks are normal. A relapse happens when you return to old habits after making positive changes. Instead of viewing relapse as failure, see it as an opportunity to learn and improve. The key to long-term diabetes prevention is preparing for challenges before they happen and getting back on track as soon as possible. Relapse Prevention Strategies:
  • Plan ahead for busy or stressful periods.
  • Identify situations that trigger unhealthy choices.
  • Develop healthier alternatives.
  • Be flexible and adjust your plans when necessary.
  • Remember that one unhealthy choice does not erase your progress.
  • Why It Matters:
  • Recognizing triggers and responding positively helps you maintain healthy habits and lowers your long-term risk of developing Type 2 diabetes.
